notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1124.tmp1124.opp-lat: Line 1: 'nec usque in horam leniant' is corrupt; read as 'horam nonam' (the ninth hour). 'ipse unus est cui nullus placeat' is obscure as transmitted; translated literally. 'quem fatu tutis beatus arguit Augustinus' is garbled; rendered 'rightly censures' (perhaps 'jure', or 'fatuitatis', 'censures for folly'). Theodore the Cappadocian is presumably Theodore Askidas. Line 2: 'quorum supra meminimus' refers to Hilary and the Fathers, though they are not mentioned earlier in this text as held. 'ipsi Donatistas ante damnaverim' is corrupt; taken as 'the Donatists had been condemned before'. 'milievantur' read as 'molirentur', 'Hilarius rech' as 'recte', and 'irude atem' as 'prudentem'. The clause on Acacius ('ut Acacium damnaret...') is syntactically loose; the bracketed '[was it right]' supplies the sense.

'Sorcius' is unidentified (possibly a corruption of another name); likewise 'Boethus', the 'blessed old man' he wrote to. 'nomine resistente' read as 'nemine resistente' (no one opposing). 'Theodotus' in the last passage read as Theodorus (Theodore of Mopsuestia). The opening clause 'quando hæc sic inhaereant' is taken as 'quando' = 'when could'; the text is somewhat corrupt. 'concesserit' near the end is read as 'should grant'; the sentence is loosely constructed. The 'judge' is Vigilius, bishop of Rome. The text breaks off after 'Cui praejudicio quo-': a portion of the text is evidently lost between 'quo-' and 'audiunt', so the final sentence is fragmentary and the subject of 'they hear' is unclear. 'abdiiari' is read as 'abdicari' (to be repudiated/disowned).

nodes.text: THE BOOK OF FACUNDUS AGAINST MOCIANUS THE SCHOLASTICUS

It would have been fitting, venerable sons, that I should dedicate this work, such as it is, which you laid upon me, to your names, as is customary. But fearing that, as people aware of our hiding places, you might fall into the false charges of the persecutors whom we are fleeing, I chose not to name you. Nor was it necessary to say this in advance for you, who are not without a share in our distress, but for others who do not know, into whose hands these pages may perhaps come. I want you to know, however, that the messenger you sent found me labouring under a serious illness, so that in such days, as he himself will be able to report to your excellency, I am not able to put off breaking my fast even to the [ninth] hour. He informed me, by your instruction, that, as our age deserves, even Mocianus now dares to find fault with the decrees of councils, and openly boasts that the bishops of Africa and of other provinces wrongly resolved to avoid the communion of those who did not shrink from attacking the Council of Chalcedon by a manifest and promulgated decree. But when do you allow us to stop, when to rest, who compel us to answer even Mocianus? But I also learned this, as the said messenger told me: that this same Mocianus, wishing to turn all the ignorant aside to the forbidden communion of the transgressors, is carrying about certain sayings of blessed Augustine; and what Augustine fittingly said against the Donatists, he himself unfittingly strives to apply to the present case, as a snare for the simple. In the same way Faustus the Gaul once, in the question of free will, by misunderstanding and wrongly applying the statements of the same blessed Augustine, deceived the unwary and led them to assent to his error; yet he was exposed and refuted by Fulgentius of Ruspe, of holy memory. But why should we wonder at this? For Augustine could not speak better than the prophets, than the apostles and evangelists; by misunderstanding and wrongly applying their words in the same way, so many heretics try to defend their errors. Yet I rejoice that, as you have reported, he now openly confesses that it was the attackers of the Church who condemned, to the prejudice of the Council of Chalcedon itself, Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, who died in the peace of the Church, and his teaching, whose praises were read out at the Council of Chalcedon with no one objecting, and also the letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, which was judged orthodox there, and the writings of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, who was found there to be a champion of the dogmatic letter of Pope Leo. For our holy brother Abbot Felix, among the very many other evils which he wrote to us about him, also reported this: that he had become a friend of Theodore the Cappadocian, and often presented him to the emperor, because he supplied him with certain chapters for condemning, after death, those who had died in the peace of the Church. And at Carthage likewise, as we have noticed, he used to maintain that the aforesaid Theodore of Mopsuestia had been justly and canonically condemned after death. Now therefore, since you have indicated that he blames what he formerly defended as right and blameless, but still asserts this, that the communion of those very attackers of the Church is to be borne, and, to confirm that assertion, misuses the words of blessed Augustine spoken against the Donatists, he has compelled me, as you wished, without regard to the strength of my health, to answer his foolish assertions in whatever way I can. For I also now lack the books for looking up the necessary testimonies, being as one put to flight and placed in hiding; because he himself is the one man whom no one pleases. But if it seems that we are like the Donatists, why is he himself not ashamed to be found like Tyconius, whom blessed Augustine rightly censures because, while reproving the Donatists for their schism, he communicated with them? Or is this man now doing anything else, when he affirms that Africa has made a schism and been separated from the Church, and yet communicates with it? And while he seems to himself the only wise man, he has become one of those of whom the Apostle says: They became vain in their thoughts, and their heart was darkened; for claiming to be wise, they became fools (Rom. 1:21). But why is it that only the Donatists, who leapt from schism into heresy, so that afterwards they also held wrong views about baptism and the divine Trinity, and not all heretics, are reproached, whether by blessed Augustine himself or by other doctors of the Church, for being unwilling to bear the wicked in the Church, unless because the Donatists separated themselves from the Church with no decrees intervening by which they might say the ancient decrees on the faith had been attacked; whereas the others, who were separated through the intervention of decrees, are blamed not for the impatience of their departure but only for their doctrine, because they would have had a just and necessary cause for departing, had they not themselves been mistaken in doctrine? Blessed Gelasius, bishop of Rome, wrote a great work against the Acephali; and neither he nor anyone else blamed them for impatience, saying that even if the definitions of the Council of Chalcedon were wrong, they ought to have borne the communion of the wicked and not separated themselves from the Church; but they are blamed for this alone, that they refused to accept sound doctrine. Why, I ask, unless because they were separated from the Church with decrees intervening, and not for other causes, as the Donatists were? Let this new doctor, then, no longer misuse, to his own and others' ruin, the arguments and examples by which the Donatists were refuted; but let him rather attend, he who, according to the prophet's saying, would not understand so as to do well (Ps. 35:4), [and see] that the case of the Donatists is one thing, and the case now being conducted another, in which we follow the examples of so many of our Fathers. For when Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, dared something against the authority of the Synod of Chalcedon, not indeed, as has now been done, by a decree established with an anathema, but only by permitting communion to the enemies of that synod, the apostolic see, foreseeing that, as the outcome showed, this relaxation tended to the destruction of the said council (for afterwards the emperor Zeno, who had ordered communion to be granted to them, leaping from lesser things to greater, spurned the council itself by a promulgated edict), condemned that same Acacius, though the aforesaid Zeno resisted. And even after his death he has been condemned up to now through the professions of bishops being ordained. But after it came about that bishops being ordained condemned in their professions Theodore of Mopsuestia with his doctrines, and the letter of Ibas, and the writings of Theodoret, the said Acacius and other adversaries of the Council of Chalcedon were withdrawn from condemnation. Since, therefore, the aforesaid Zeno, despising the decrees of the apostolic see, was in communion with the aforesaid Acacius, and compelled all the Churches established within the bounds of his realm to do the same, and then Anastasius succeeded to the empire and to a like presumption, the whole East, except for very few who lay hidden in that multitude, remained cut off from the communion of the apostolic see for nearly forty years, until the time of Justin. And when certain bishops of that region during that time asked for the communion of the apostolic see for themselves and their Churches, they did not obtain it until, in the time of the emperor Justin, they subscribed to the condemnation of Acacius. Yet none of them said: We are not tares, but we tolerate the tares, lest we root up the wheat along with them. And why would they not also have said this to the apostolic see, if that comparison fitted such cases too: Rather, we act rightly, we remain in the commandments of the Gospel, we who tolerate the tares, rather than you, who on account of the tares have rooted up the wheat along with them, or have departed from the wheat? What then shall we say here, religious sons? Through the course of so many years, was no one found among the Roman bishops, from Felix, who condemned Acacius, to Hormisdas, who reconciled the Churches of the East, among whom was blessed Gelasius, proclaimed throughout the whole world with the glory of a most renowned fame for holiness of life and learning, was no one found either in the Roman clergy, while the Christian people lived there, or in all the western Churches, who was even as concerned for the unity of the Churches as this new master sent in these latest times, so that no one knew and taught that in that same case too the communion of the wicked was to be tolerated, lest the wheat be rooted up with the tares? If it is right to believe that the knowledge and discipline of preserving unity began with blessed Augustine, whose writings, fitting against the Donatists, this man now unfittingly applies to the present case. And so Hilary, illustrious doctor of the Churches, and the other more ancient Fathers with him whom we mentioned above, did not observe what pertains to the safeguarding of unity, in that, before anything was decreed against the Council of Nicaea, they withdrew themselves from the communion of those who were plotting these things. Although, as we said, the Donatists had been condemned before, still, had the apostolic see too, when afterwards it condemned Acacius for the violated decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, while Zeno resisted, not read these and similar writings of blessed Augustine? Even if it should be thought less able to understand by itself what pertains to the observance of unity, [was it right] that it condemned Acacius, whom the emperor would not allow to be expelled without much wheat? Nor, then, ought the Roman Church to have reconciled the Churches of the East and received them into communion upon due satisfaction; but rather the Churches of the East, which had tolerated the tares, ought to have reconciled the Roman Church, separated from the wheat. Or was this not done because this man could not yet teach through the catholic Church as he does now? Or rather because he who wishes to bring this perverse and confused doctrine into the catholic Church, and would that it were not coloured with the name of Augustine, had not yet come to it? For he wants the apostolic see, which then forgave others their fault, to have been itself rather guilty, together with the rest who upheld its sentence on Acacius, as if for having made a schism; and, sparing no one, as is his way, he wants those Easterners too, who were forgiven at their own request, to appear to have been converted to schismatic Westerners, whom they themselves ought to have converted to themselves. And these things would indeed suffice us for refuting him, if the adversaries, whom he himself blames, not pronouncing an anathema on the Council of Chalcedon nor on all of us, but merely doing something against its authority, had rather been condemned by us under anathema. But now, since they act impiously, and anathematize us and our Fathers, and by this anathema separate themselves from the whole Church of Christ, we who by God's guidance stand firm in the judgement and communion of our fathers, we, I say, in the Church on which they laid an anathema, have resolved, according to the observance of the Christian religion, not to communicate with those separated from the Church. I would not, then, grant this man even this, that we have done what Hilary rightly did with his colleagues, who, when no decree had yet gone forth to the prejudice of the Council of Nicaea, but the opponents had ventured their first schemes, hastened to separate themselves from their communion. I would not grant him that the African Church separated itself from the attackers of the Council of Chalcedon, but rather that it avoided communicating with those already separated. Hence someone more diligent and more fervent in zeal for God could, on the example of Hilary, more justly blame us for slowness than Mocianus could accuse us of schism or of haste. Who, moreover, unless senseless and wise in his own eyes, and, as the Apostle says, vainly puffed up by the mind of his flesh (Col. 2:18), against the judgement of the whole Church, not regarding even the outcome of events that followed, would dare to reproach Hilary, a prudent and moderate governor of the Church, who could not bear to communicate even by letter with the bishops of Gaul themselves, because he believed that in so great a case they had kept silent and had not resisted the adversaries? Or who, not daring to reproach him, would reproach the African Church with levity or impatience, which, only when it saw the Council of Chalcedon, and all who hold its judgement, anathematized by a decree now openly promulgated, avoided communicating with the condemners of its Fathers and of itself, not as though contrary to Augustine's teaching against the Donatists, but following Hilary's practice against the attackers of a universal synod? And that you may know how, with the help of God who rules and directs us, we follow Augustine and Hilary in harmony, and do not set them against each other as if contrary, so as to approve the one and disapprove the other, but follow each according to the difference of the cases, hear what, among other things, I argued at the trial before Vigilius himself, as the acts of the third session, issued to us by the office, show. 'I ask,' I said, 'of your justice that you inquire whether the letter of Ibas, which has been condemned as Nestorian, was received by the Synod of Chalcedon; and when it has been established that what the opposing party puts forward about the person of Theodore does not harm the synod, then permit what they wish to bring forward to be read, lest perhaps the proceedings should seem to amount to a re-examination of the said synod. For I confess plainly to your blessedness that it was not on account of the condemnation of Theodore of Mopsuestia that I withdrew from the communion of those who oppose [us]. For this, even if it is not to be approved, I nevertheless think is to be borne, and I do not judge it so great a cause that we ought to be separated from the communion of the multitude on its account. But because from the person of Theodore they have tried to prove the letter of Ibas Nestorian, and from the letter of Ibas to discredit the synod by which it was received.' In these words of mine, then, you recognise first of all that I was concerned for the standing of the general synod, lest, as the Acephali always sought, its authority should be brought into re-examination and broken. Next, see that we do not now learn from this man that the wicked are to be borne for the sake of the Church's unity, as Augustine taught. For when I said: For I confess plainly to your blessedness that it was not on account of the condemnation of Theodore of Mopsuestia that I withdrew from the communion of those who oppose [us]; for this, even if it is not to be approved, I nevertheless think is to be borne, and I do not judge it so great a cause that we ought to be separated from the communion of the multitude on its account, I showed that I was mindful of the teaching of Augustine. But since I also ought not to be contrary to Hilary and his colleagues, who, though they doubtless bore many wicked men in the Churches and condemned schismatics, nevertheless did not judge that those heads of Churches were to be borne who tried by their decrees to break the authority of the general synods by which the Church is defended, for that reason I went on to add, saying that I had avoided their communion because from the person of Theodore they had tried to prove Nestorian the letter of Ibas, in which his teaching is praised, and from the letter of Ibas to discredit the synod by which it was received. For what other cause must be said to have existed, that a bishop who died in the peace of the Church should be condemned with his doctrines a hundred and twenty years after his death, or a letter whose author is said to be uncertain? For they do not even admit that it is Ibas's, but [only] that it is said to be his. Or why should the subscription of so many bishops be sought for this, unless because the consent not of a few but of a multitude could prejudice the whole council? And since the judge pretended not to know this, I asked and at the same time said: 'Order me therefore first to demonstrate this, so that I may show that it is falsely denied that [the letter] was received by the holy Synod of Chalcedon, and may refute all the fabrications of the opponents by which they condemned it as impious, to the destruction of the Synod of Chalcedon.' But since he was bound by a secret promise made before the trial, in which he pledged that he would condemn these same chapters, so that he might clear himself as if through ignorance, he did not allow me to make the proof which I was offering, and which he himself ought to have insistently demanded. But the minutes by which the case had begun to be opened were removed from the middle, and his own trial was broken off; he then demanded of the bishops sitting with him that each should set down in writing, as his reply, what he thought about the case put before them. And because those bishops had mostly come to Constantinople to meet him on his arrival, and no subscription of theirs was held in this case, and they had been confident of their own integrity, on the pretext of this inquiry they too were compelled, separately, by the adversaries of the Church to answer as those adversaries dictated, to the prejudice of the great council. And so that they might not afterwards withdraw, and fail to present to the trial what they had answered in writing, they were now openly led to him under the escort and guard of those same men to hand over their profane and detestable answers. We saw these things with our own eyes. We beheld the Acephali, eager and exultant in the presence of the judge himself, when they brought bishops to him carrying those same answers. And when could these things stick in the hearts of those who hear of them in such a way that you could detest and lament them as we do, in whose minds the image of these very evils still lingers? He, receiving the answers mentioned, after some days took them to the palace and handed them to the other party, to be kept, to the prejudice of the Synod of Chalcedon, together with the signed statements of the others who had subscribed earlier. But so that he might not appear to his own people to be a betrayer, he deceived them with words such as these, saying: Why do we keep these answers, which are contrary to the Synod of Chalcedon, with us, so that, if they are found some day in the archive of the Roman Church, they may be believed to have been approved by us? Let us rather take them to the palace, and let them deal with them: they themselves will know [what to do]. As if he could not tear them up or burn them himself, or annul them by his own sentence, or give them back to those by whom they had been given: answers which he ought neither to have accepted from them nor extorted, if he truly guarded against prejudice to the general synod. And by this customary pretence, pretending that he was guarding against prejudice to it, he did, according to the wishes of its opponents, what will prejudice it if we pass over it. For how would it not prejudice it, if about seventy bishops gathered at Constantinople with the Roman bishop, to say nothing of those who had subscribed earlier, are shown to have condemned, together with those who approved it, the letter approved by the Council of Chalcedon? and to have anathematised after his death, together with his doctrines, that bishop whose praises for his teaching were read out in the said Council of Chalcedon with no one opposing, while the rest knew it and remained in their communion? For this reason, then, it was necessary not only to withdraw ourselves from their communion, but also, since those who first yielded to this prejudice at the emperor's command seemed to hold the more powerful place in the Church, lest their opinion should seem the one rather to be held, to recall, as we have done elsewhere, how Menas of Constantinople, Zoilus of Alexandria, Ephraem of Antioch and Peter of Jerusalem, before they either consented or yielded, testified that it ought not to be done. For this reason also we thought it necessary not to keep silent about the signed statements of the Roman bishop himself, made to the other party, either earlier at the impulse of ambition, when he was burning to be made bishop, or later out of venality, lest the true faith should suffer prejudice through the authority of his name. But if this had not happened, and he himself had not earlier anathematised the whole Church, we ought to have kept his opinion in him, and to have followed the example of ancient integrity which he gave us. For before he too committed this, writing on his journey to the bishop of Constantinople, who first assented to the prejudice against the great synod, but whom he anticipated with his letter, he says: 'Therefore we have thought it right to make known that our lord and son the most clement emperor has urged us, through the illustrious Leo, in most serene words, to keep, with you and with all our brothers and fellow bishops, and to guard with stable firmness, the peace which Christ, our Lord God and Saviour, loves above all burnt offerings. We gladly embrace this exhortation of the most pious prince. But if you wisely attend to the good of peace, as befits the place of your priesthood, you must both notice and proclaim what peace is to be held in the Church of God, since the Apostle, who declared that our Lord spoke in him, says: May the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your understandings (Philippians 4:7). And Christ our God himself, wishing to show the marks of perfect peace, says: My peace I leave to you, my peace I give to you: not as the world gives do I give to you (John 14:27). For what kind [of peace] the world can give, he himself teaches us through the prophet who says: Saying, peace, peace, when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14). And let us weigh this by a like reasoning, that in the Acts of the Apostles it is declared concerning perfect peace, about those who believed in the Lord, that there was in them one heart and one soul (Acts 4:32). There are, then, many writings we may find by which earthly and heavenly peace are to be distinguished. But since we do not believe you are ignorant of them, let it suffice to have drawn out a few out of very many, so that the judgement of your fraternity may rather assess what peace ought chiefly to be held by bishops.' Is it not plain, and does it not evidently appear from what we have recalled, that even the very opponents who disagree with us in many things nevertheless agree in this, that in such cases the communion of transgressors is to be avoided? and that that peace is to be held by the bishops of God in the Church which does not overturn the standing of the Church itself? And it is overturned if its general decisions on the faith are broken, on any pretext, by the decrees of other bishops. On this account, too, when he came to the royal city he suspended from communion those who had communicated with such men. And again he says in his letter mentioned above: 'Since it is not unknown to us that the deacon Stephen, then the representative of our Church, over which by the grace of God we preside, suspended himself, along with very many Christians, from your communion for as long as he lived; and while we were staying in the island of Sicily we learned, from the report of our brother and fellow bishop Datius, that he and other fellow bishops of ours, and many Christian sons of the Church, had likewise withdrawn themselves from your communion; and when we inquired into the causes of the scandal that had arisen, our aforesaid brother and fellow bishop answered that your fraternity's person had done what had not been committed for any reason in the times of any of your predecessors or ours.' Do you see that not only this judge and his deacon, but also Datius, bishop of Milan, with other bishops, considered that the communion of such transgressors was not to be borne? Why then is any question still raised against us about this, on which there is neither any contradiction among those who contradict one another, nor any disagreement among those who disagree in many things? For the judge asserts that he issued that judgement unwillingly. We on the contrary reply that he sinned of his own accord, having made a promise out of ambition, and endured no torments to which he could be believed to have yielded. And while he asserts that he did this unwillingly, he says again in the same place that he did it in ignorance. But we prove that he could not have done in ignorance what he asserts he committed unwillingly. After this he also wishes to appear to have done nothing to the prejudice of the Council of Chalcedon. Against him we set his own excuses: for unless he had done something that prejudiced it, he would by no means strive to clear and absolve himself, either by the violence of the princes or by his own ignorance. Since, then, there is found to be much disagreement among us about these and other matters, there is nevertheless agreement between the parties on this point, and it stands among all without any controversy, that in such cases the communion of transgressors is to be avoided. Finally, not even Sorcius, the chief ornament of their party, and who ought to be nowhere but with such men, contradicts this opinion; rather he even says something more. For writing to the blessed old man Boethus, before he set sail to take back what he had condemned, he pronounced against them an anathema, which the African councils did not do, saying: 'I anathematise Eutyches with all his followers and helpers, whoever attempt to infringe in anything the tome of the holy Council of Chalcedon; and whoever anathematises the letter of Ibas which that holy Council of Chalcedon received is anathema to me.' Accordingly, if Mocianus is displeased with the observance, in the similar case of the Council of Nicaea, of Hilary and his other colleagues, through whom the orthodox faith was preserved in that storm and reached us undefiled; if he is displeased also with the solicitude and caution of the holy and most learned orthodox man Jerome; if he is displeased with the example given us long ago, in the case of the Council of Chalcedon too, in Acacius, by so many prelates of the apostolic see, and confirmed by the consent of the universal Church; if he is displeased with what the African councils have decided in the present assault on that same council; if he is displeased with what the bishops of other provinces too, such as those of Illyricum and Dalmatia, saw should be done: let him at least be pleased with what Vigilius himself, or what Sorcius himself, held: that in cases of this kind the communion of such transgressors is to be avoided. For this reason too blessed Stephen, prelate of the apostolic see, when he learned that holy Cyprian and other African bishops had decreed that all heretics should be baptised, although, as has been said, they had issued such an opinion without interposing any anathema, and neither against any older decrees of a general council nor in connivance with heretics, nevertheless at once declared to him that if any dared to do this they would be driven out of the Church: and the Church holds the opinion of Stephen rather than of Cyprian, not only that heretics are not to be rebaptised, but also that those who rebaptise are not to be tolerated. But that most prudent man Augustine, to refute the Donatists for their schism, who try to defend by the authority of blessed Cyprian the sacrilege by which they repeat baptism, believed his example sufficient: because, although he thought otherwise about baptism than very many bishops of other provinces, he nevertheless did not separate himself from the Church as the Donatists themselves did. And he would have separated himself, if he had decreed an anathema between himself and those who disagreed. This example of blessed Cyprian, therefore, does nothing to help this man's assertion, as you see; but you ought to see how it rather helps us. We say, then, that just as, although we condemn the rebaptising Donatists as separated from the Church, we do not condemn Cyprian and his associates, who did not divide themselves from the Church by interposing any anathema when they decreed about baptism what now seems to have given occasion to the error of the Donatists, so, although we condemn the Nestorians as separated from the Church, we do not condemn Theodore of Mopsuestia, who did not divide [himself] from the Church by interposing any anathema, even if he wrote something which perhaps now seems to have given occasion to the error of the Nestorians. And just as it suffices us to reject the opinions of Cyprian and his associates on baptism, and not to condemn them under anathema, so, if Theodore perhaps wrote something badly through lack of understanding, it suffices us to reject it, and not to condemn it under anathema: since the Church has always shown this reverence to those who died in the reward of her peace and in honour, that she condemned under anathema, as she does heretics, neither those who had perhaps erred in such questions through the ignorance of human weakness, nor even their very sayings. For it is not the ignorance of human weakness but obstinacy that makes a heretic. Hence blessed Augustine in the book On Catechising the Uninstructed says: 'Although even those who departed from this life as catholics, and left some Christian writings to posterity, in certain places of their works, either through not being understood or, as is human weakness, being less able with the sharpness of the mind to penetrate hidden things, and straying from the truth through what resembled it, have been an occasion to presumptuous and bold men for contriving and begetting some heresy.' So the catholic Augustine says that those departed this life as catholics who, being established in the Church, through human weakness were less able with the sharpness of the mind to penetrate hidden things, and strayed from the truth through what resembled it; nor does he wish them to be called heretics, although they were an occasion to presumptuous and bold men for contriving and begetting some heresy. And therefore we do not call heretics blessed Cyprian and his colleagues, who through human weakness erred in the question of baptism, or Theodore of Mopsuestia, if he should be shown perhaps to have strayed from the truth in something and to have departed this life while in that error, since we do not deny that they remained in the catholic Church to the end. In vain, therefore, did this man, as he was wont, gather for himself some examples or other not pertaining to the case, by which he strove to prove that the oft-mentioned Theodore of Mopsuestia was justly and canonically condemned. For if some bishop is to be condemned who at his death made a heretic heir to his property by testament, it is not that he was unable to penetrate hidden things with the sharpness of the mind so as to do this, or strayed from the truth through what resembled it; but he committed a manifest crime, not through the ignorance of weakness, but through the depravity of the will. Hence it is that for Philip, who said: Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us (John 14:8), having failed for so long a time to know Christ passed without punishment. But the offence committed shortly before by Ananias and Sapphira, who kept back part of the price of their land, was immediately followed by the penalty of death. Thus the simple ignorance of piety is judged one way by the Lord, and the double conscience of depravity another. And indeed the apostolic see, through blessed Gelasius, judges it wrong to condemn after death anyone who died in the peace of the Church, when he says: 'What is beyond the measure of our power let us leave to divine judgement. And they will not be able to charge us with the offence of transgression if we remit to the living what is possible for the Church, by God's gift, who demand that we give even to the dead either pardon or condemnation, which it is manifest is not possible for us: for since it is said: Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven (Matthew 18:18), those who are known to be no longer on earth he has reserved not to human judgement but to his own. Nor does the Church dare to claim for herself what she sees was not granted to the blessed apostles themselves. For if it is permitted to bind the dead, it is permitted also to loose them; and if it is permitted to inflict condemnation on the dead, it is permitted also to give pardon.' But if perhaps someone thinks that that opinion should be held by which some who died in the peace of the Church are believed to be condemnable, and not rather this one of the apostolic see, which understands that these things are reserved to divine judgement alone, and should grant that, since if it is permitted to bind the dead it is permitted also to loose them, and if it is permitted to inflict condemnation on the dead it is permitted also to give pardon: it does not follow that he should therefore also think that Theodore of Mopsuestia is to be condemned. For that opinion does not strike at those who, like blessed Cyprian and his associates, through human weakness were less able with the sharpness of the mind to penetrate hidden things and strayed from the truth through what resembled it, but rather at those who are proved to have sinned knowingly and willingly. Moreover it is also known that judgement was given on this case of Theodore at the time when the Apollinarists, the forebears of the Acephali, sought to have him repudiated together with certain chapters from his sayings, and were repulsed by John of Antioch and the eastern council, and also by Cyril of Alexandria and Proclus of Constantinople. But now, to the prejudice of the great Synod of Chalcedon, the question about him is revived, though it was settled a hundred and twenty years ago and already given over to oblivion.
